clinicalPearls: A major cause of preventable childhood blindness and increased infection-related mortality in low- and middle-income countries.
The earliest and most sensitive symptom is night blindness, reflecting impaired rod photoreceptor function.
Progressive ocular signs (xerophthalmia) include conjunctival dryness, Bitot spots, corneal xerosis, and ultimately corneal ulceration and keratomalacia that can rapidly destroy the eye.
Deficiency also impairs epithelial integrity and immune function, increasing severity of infections such as measles and diarrhoeal disease.
It commonly coexists with protein-energy malnutrition and other micronutrient deficiencies.
Measles can precipitate acute deficiency and corneal damage, so supplementation is recommended during measles infection in at-risk children.
Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by a low serum retinol level and dietary history.
High-dose vitamin A supplementation reverses early ocular signs and reduces mortality, and periodic supplementation programmes are a key public health measure.
Excessive vitamin A intake is toxic, so dosing schedules must be followed carefully.
reference.pathophysiology: Vitamin A (retinol) is essential for the visual cycle, where its aldehyde form retinal combines with opsin to form rhodopsin in rod cells; deficiency reduces rhodopsin regeneration and causes night blindness. Retinoic acid also regulates differentiation and maintenance of epithelial tissues and mucosal barriers, so deficiency leads to squamous metaplasia and keratinisation of conjunctival and corneal epithelium (xerophthalmia) and of other epithelia. Impaired epithelial barriers and immune regulation increase susceptibility to and severity of infection.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of night blindness (retinitis pigmentosa)
Fat malabsorption syndromes (cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease, coeliac disease)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical ocular examination for Bitot spots, xerosis, and corneal changes
Assessment of nutritional status and dietary intake
Investigation for fat malabsorption where suspected
redFlags: Corneal ulceration or keratomalacia threatening irreversible blindness
Rapidly progressing ocular signs, particularly during measles
Severe concurrent infection in a malnourished child
reference.prognosis: Early ocular changes are fully reversible with prompt supplementation, but corneal ulceration and keratomalacia can cause permanent blindness; adequate vitamin A status also lowers infection-related mortality.
pitfalls: Overlooking night blindness as an early, treatable warning sign
Failing to supplement vitamin A during measles in at-risk children
Missing underlying fat malabsorption in a child with deficiency and adequate intake
Causing toxicity by exceeding recommended supplementation doses
management: Prompt oral vitamin A (retinol) supplementation, given as an age-based course, to reverse deficiency and halt progression of xerophthalmia
Vitamin A supplementation during measles infection in at-risk children to prevent acute deficiency and corneal damage
Ophthalmic care of corneal xerosis, ulceration and keratomalacia with topical lubrication and antibiotics to prevent secondary infection and preserve sight
Dietary improvement with vitamin A-rich foods and treatment of coexisting protein-energy malnutrition and other micronutrient deficiencies
Investigate and manage underlying fat malabsorption where present
Population prevention through periodic supplementation programmes and food fortification in endemic regions
Monitor serum retinol and perform regular ocular examination to track recovery
